subject: Computer Networking
title: Cookies and Sessions
description: A quick win: understand Cookies and Sessions.

hook.text: HTTP forgets you instantly. Cookies are small files that make the stateless web remember who you are.

buildup.text: A server sends a Set-Cookie header. The browser stores the cookie and sends it with every future request.

discovery.text: Session cookies expire when you close the browser. Persistent cookies survive for days, months, or years.

twist.text: Third-party cookies track you across sites. Ad networks use them to build profiles. Privacy disaster.

climax.text: Chrome is phasing out third-party cookies. Privacy Sandbox aims to replace them with less invasive APIs.

punchline.text: Cookies add memory to a forgetful protocol. Useful, but privacy-risky.

quiz.question: Why are third-party cookies a privacy concern?
options: They let ad networks track users across multiple websites
They slow down page load times significantly
They can execute malicious code on your computer

details.summary: Cookies are small data packets that servers store in browsers to maintain state across HTTP's stateless request model. Session cookies track login status, preference cookies remember settings, and tracking cookies follow users across sites. Privacy regulations now require transparent cookie consent.
details.whyItMatters: Cookies are the primary mechanism for maintaining user sessions on the web. Understanding their security attributes and privacy implications is essential for web development.
takeaways: Cookies maintain state across stateless HTTP requests
HttpOnly and Secure flags protect cookies from common attacks
SameSite attribute limits cross-site cookie transmission

faq.question: What are the security risks of cookies?
faq.answer: Cross-site scripting can steal cookies if HttpOnly is not set. Cross-site request forgery uses cookies to perform unauthorized actions. Session hijacking intercepts cookies to impersonate users. Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite attributes mitigate these risks.

faq.question: What is the SameSite cookie attribute?
faq.answer: SameSite controls whether cookies are sent with cross-site requests. Strict sends cookies only to the same site. Lax allows cookies on top-level navigations like clicking a link. None allows all cross-site requests but requires Secure. Chrome defaults to Lax, blocking most cross-site cookie abuse.
